clinicalPearls: A standard drink contains roughly 10-12 g of ethanol; one typical drink raises the blood ethanol level by about 0.02 g/dL (Harrison 22e p.3675).

Behavioral, psychomotor and cognitive impairment appears at only 0.02-0.04 g/dL (one to two drinks); 'legal intoxication' in most U.S. states is 0.08 g/dL, with 0.04 g/dL applied to pilots and to drivers in some countries (Harrison 22e p.3676).

In a person without tolerance, light coma with depressed vital signs occurs around 0.30 g/dL and death between 0.30 and 0.40 g/dL; alcohol probably causes more overdose deaths than any other drug (Harrison 22e p.3676).

Heavy drinking while fasting can cause transient hypoglycemia within 6-36 h by suppressing gluconeogenesis, producing temporarily abnormal glucose tolerance that can be misread as diabetes until 2-4 weeks of abstinence (Harrison 22e p.3675).

Most ethanol is metabolized in the liver: the cytosolic alcohol dehydrogenase pathway generates acetaldehyde (then cleared by aldehyde dehydrogenase), while the microsomal ethanol-oxidizing system (MEOS) handles >=10% at high blood levels (Harrison 22e p.3675).
Blackouts (temporary anterograde amnesia while awake) occur in about 35% of drinkers, with en bloc blackouts at levels >0.20 and fragmentary blackouts at >0.12 (Harrison 22e p.3676).

Alcohol disrupts sleep architecture, reducing early-night REM and deep sleep and relaxing pharyngeal muscles to worsen snoring and apnea; sleep apnea symptoms occur in about 75% of men with AUD aged >=60 (Harrison 22e p.3676).
DSM-5 diagnoses AUD when >=2 of 11 criteria cluster in the same 12-month period; severity is mild (2-3), moderate (4-5) or severe (>=6 items) (Harrison 22e p.3677-3678).

Roughly 60% of the risk for AUD is genetic; a flushing response (ALDH variant seen in Japanese, Chinese and Korean individuals) lowers risk, while a low level of response to alcohol predicts future heavy drinking and problems (Harrison 22e p.3678).

Useful blood markers of regular heavy intake are GGT (>35 U) and carbohydrate-deficient transferrin (CDT >20 U/L or >2.6%), with the combination more accurate than either alone; high-normal MCV (>=91) and elevated uric acid also support the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.3678-3679).
Continued heavy drinking shortens life span by about 10 years, with leading causes of early death being heart disease, cancer, accidents and suicide (Harrison 22e p.3678).

'Holiday heart' refers to atrial or ventricular arrhythmias, especially paroxysmal tachycardia, occurring temporarily after heavy drinking in people with no other evidence of heart disease (Harrison 22e p.3677).
harrison.pathophysiology: Ethanol is a CNS depressant that acutely enhances GABA activity (notably at GABA-A receptors) and inhibits postsynaptic NMDA excitatory glutamate receptors; chronic exposure produces compensatory downregulation of GABA-related activity and upregulation of NMDA receptor subunits. Falling blood levels after chronic use therefore unmask a hyperexcitable state, explaining withdrawal phenomena. Acute alcohol raises dopamine in the ventral tegmentum and nucleus accumbens, releases beta-endorphins, and increases serotonin and stress hormones (cortisol, ACTH), driving reward, craving and relapse. Cellular (pharmacodynamic), metabolic (up to ~30% faster hepatic metabolism after 1-2 weeks) and learned/behavioral mechanisms contribute to acquired tolerance. Cellular adaptations may take weeks to resolve, so rapid drops in blood level produce withdrawal that is most intense in the first 5 days but with protracted symptoms (disturbed sleep, anxiety) lasting up to 4-6 months (Harrison 22e p.3675-3676).
additionalDifferentials: Alcohol ketoacidosis versus diabetic ketoacidosis (alcohol-related shows raised ketones, only mild glucose elevation, large anion gap, mild-moderate lactate rise, beta-hydroxybutyrate/lactate ratio between 2:1 and 9:1) (Harrison 22e p.3675)

Substance-induced mood, anxiety or psychotic disorder versus an independent primary psychiatric disorder; about 40% of those with AUD meet criteria for a major depressive episode but roughly half are substance-induced and resolve within a month of abstinence (Harrison 22e p.3676-3677)
Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome and alcohol-related cognitive impairment versus other dementias; there is no single 'alcoholic dementia' entity (Harrison 22e p.3676)
Peripheral neuropathy of alcohol versus diabetic neuropathy (both bilateral, distal, with numbness, tingling, paresthesias) (Harrison 22e p.3676)
nonInfectiousMimics: Diabetes mellitus (alcohol-induced transient hypoglycemia and abnormal glucose tolerance) (Harrison 22e p.3675)
Primary depressive, anxiety or psychotic disorder (alcohol-induced psychiatric symptoms during intoxication/withdrawal) (Harrison 22e p.3675, 3676-3677)
additionalInvestigations: Gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT >35 U) - marker of heavy consumption (Harrison 22e p.3678)
Carbohydrate-deficient transferrin (CDT >20 U/L or >2.6%); combined with GGT for higher accuracy (Harrison 22e p.3679)
Mean corpuscular volume (high-normal >=91) and serum uric acid (>7 mg/dL) (Harrison 22e p.3679)
Blood ethanol level (e.g., 100 mg/dL = 0.10 g/dL) (Harrison 22e p.3675)
Toxicology screen for other CNS depressants (benzodiazepines) and opioids in severe intoxication (Harrison 22e p.3679)
AUDIT 10-item screening questionnaire (score >=8 may indicate harmful use) - screening only, not diagnostic (Harrison 22e p.3679-3680)
MRI/CT may show ventricular enlargement and widened cortical sulci in ~50% of long-term AUD, usually reversible with abstinence (Harrison 22e p.3676)
redFlags: Withdrawal seizure (about 2% of patients), with higher risk in older age, concomitant medical problems, polydrug misuse and larger alcohol quantities (Harrison 22e p.3680)
Withdrawal delirium / delirium tremens (about 1%): agitated delirium with confusion, fluctuating consciousness, tremor and marked autonomic overactivity (Harrison 22e p.3680)
Autonomic overactivity during withdrawal: rising pulse, respiratory rate, sweating and body temperature (Harrison 22e p.3680)
Severe intoxication with respiratory depression, cardiac arrhythmias or blood pressure instability; light coma near 0.30 g/dL and death 0.30-0.40 g/dL (Harrison 22e p.3676, 3679)
Gastrointestinal bleeding from hemorrhagic gastritis or a Mallory-Weiss tear after violent vomiting (Harrison 22e p.3677)
Pregnancy: any drinking risks fetal alcohol spectrum disorder; complete abstinence advised (Harrison 22e p.3677)
harrison.prognosis: With at least a year of follow-up after treatment, more than half of people with AUD achieve a marked reduction in drinking and related problems or full abstinence, and even without formal treatment or self-help groups there is at least a 20% chance of spontaneous long-term remission. Many alcohol-related organ changes are reversible with abstinence: blood pressure normalizes within weeks, GGT/CDT return toward normal within weeks, thrombocytopenia usually resolves within a week (unless cirrhosis or congestive splenomegaly), MRI/CT brain changes generally reverse, and acute myopathy improves though may not fully remit. Continued heavy drinking shortens life span by roughly 10 years, mainly through heart disease, cancer, accidents and suicide (Harrison 22e p.3677-3678).
pitfalls: Misreading alcohol-induced transient hypoglycemia/abnormal glucose tolerance as diabetes before 2-4 weeks of abstinence (Harrison 22e p.3675)
Misdiagnosing alcohol ketoacidosis as diabetic ketosis (Harrison 22e p.3675)

Treating substance-induced psychiatric symptoms with long-term medication when they typically resolve within days to ~4 weeks of abstinence (only short-term antipsychotics for substance-induced psychosis are usually needed) (Harrison 22e p.3676-3677)

Giving routine IV fluids in withdrawal - most patients are normally hydrated or mildly overhydrated, so fluids should be avoided unless there is a specific medical indication, bleeding, vomiting or diarrhea (Harrison 22e p.3680)
Relying on questionnaires (e.g., AUDIT) alone - they are screening tools and a face-to-face interview is required for diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.3679)
A false-negative tuberculin skin test from impaired delayed-hypersensitivity in chronic heavy drinkers (Harrison 22e p.3677)
Assuming AUD spares affluent or professional patients - lifetime risk among physicians is similar to the general population (Harrison 22e p.3678)
harrison.severityClassification: DSM-5 alcohol use disorder severity by number of criteria endorsed in a 12-month period: mild = 2-3 items, moderate = 4-5 items, severe = >=6 of the 11 items (Harrison 22e p.3678). Effects of blood alcohol levels without tolerance (Table 464-1): 0.02 decreased inhibitions; 0.08 reduced complex cognition and motor performance; 0.20 slurred speech, incoordination, poor judgment; 0.30 light coma with depressed vital signs; 0.40 death (Harrison 22e p.3676).
